body.text: The migration changes Tony Burke announced at the National Press Club on Thursday target temporary migration, especially international students and working holidaymakers. Burke organised his speech around three questions: who arrives, who stays and who leaves? His adjustments to visa settings aim to reduce the number of backpackers and students arriving in Australia, and increase the number departing, to help the government bring net overseas migration down to 225,000 people before the 2028 election.

The changes fall well short of a comprehensive overhaul of a migration system — a system that Labor described as “fundamentally broken” after it took office in 2022. And, by focusing on temporary migration, Burke has left untouched some of the festering issues in the permanent migration program, particularly in the family stream.
Data obtained by Inside Story shows two things: reform of the family migration program is urgently needed, and the government’s options are heavily constrained.

Family migration is better understood as partner and parent migration, for these two groups dominate the intake. Eight out of ten family visas in the permanent migration program are reserved for the spouses and de facto partners of Australian citizens and permanent residents, while more than one in ten are set aside for parents. The remainder go to dependent children and “other family.”
With demand for visas massively exceeding supply, the family stream is overwhelmed by processing backlogs. This causes headaches for government and acute distress for families.

Let’s start with the partner visa, which enables someone to live in Australia for two years and serves as a stepping stone to permanent migration if the relationship endures. On 30 June 2026, 117,000 people were waiting in the queue for a partner visa, a number that has doubled in three years.

When the pandemic closed Australia’s borders, the queue for partner visas almost halved. Applications for permanent migration fell and the government shifted places from the skilled stream to the family stream, granting visas to partners who were already in Australia. But when borders reopened, demand rose, and places were shifted back to the skilled stream. With fewer partner visas on offer, demand outstripped supply and the backlog of pending applications rocketed to a record high.

The Albanese government’s “nominal” planning level for partners stayed unchanged at 40,500 places during its first three years, and Home Affairs delivered almost exactly that number of visas. This year the planning level for partners was marginally increased to 41,500 places, but unless the government grants far more visas or finds some way to cull applications the log jam will only get bigger.

Different visa subclasses apply depending on whether applicants are already in Australia or are overseas. Two-thirds of all applications in the queue were lodged onshore, and the median processing time for this visa is now seventeen months. That means half the applications are finalised within this time and half take longer. For the two offshore visas the median processing times are thirteen months and fifteen months.
When processing delays were this severe in 2020, Labor backbencher Julian Hill slammed the Coalition government for its cruel and illegal actions.

Cruel because couples could be separated for years and unable to build their futures together. “Relationships are now stressed or broken as waiting times continue to increase,” Hill told parliament. “Australians now cannot plan their lives. Do they buy a house? Sell a house? Do they start a family? Will they ever get a visa?”
Illegal because Hill claimed the government had put “a hard cap” on the number of partner visas issued every year, which isn’t permitted under the Migration Act.

“Hard caps” are allowed in most visa categories, and Home Affairs halts processing applications as soon as they are hit. Remaining applications are then stuck in an unmoving queue until processing resumes under the next year’s cap. Parliament has twice prevented governments from capping and queuing partner visas in this way — acknowledging, as Hill told parliament in 2020, “the reasonable right of Australians to fall in love and build a life with their partner here.”

The application backlog under Labor is now worse than it was under the “miserable” Morrison government Hill railed against, and Hill is now assistant minister for citizenship, customs and multicultural affairs.
So has Labor implemented a “hard cap”? Is it acting illegally? The answer to that question turns on legalese.

Home Affairs says partner visas are “demand driven.” Common sense would take this to mean that cases are processed as they are received, so the number of visas will rise (or fall) in line with the number of valid applications submitted. But this isn’t what happens. Instead, visa outcomes match the planning level because Home Affairs has a less straightforward understanding of “demand driven”.

The most recent report on the administration of the migration program notes that section 87 of the Migration Act prevents partner visas being capped, but adds: “In administering the program, the department considers planning levels and prioritises processing resources accordingly.” (My emphasis.)

After I wrote about these issues last year, an insider translated the bureaucratese for me. While the Migration Act exempts partner visas from being subjected to a hard cap, they told me, Home Affairs sees no legal barrier to allocating resources (staff and time, that is) to issuing only the number of visas set by the government’s planning level. Even though the law prevents explicit legislative limits on partner visas, the department is confident it can safely hold numbers down by administrative means.

The insider acknowledged that this view may prove wrong if challenged in court. For now, though, thinking inside the department, and advice to ministers, is not shaped by concerns about the legality of restricting visas in this way to align with planning levels.

Back in 2020, Julian Hill told parliament that the problems with partner visas couldn’t be wished away. “The numbers will just keep rising,” he said. “Clear the backlog of partner visas and let Australians who are in love be reunited with their partners. It’s not too much to ask.”

Turns out, though, it is too much to ask. Why? First, because Pauline Hanson is on the attack and Labor refuses to give her ammunition by issuing more partner visas and increasing the size of the permanent migration program.

Second, both major parties are committed to reserving two-thirds of permanent migration spots for skilled migrants. So the government is reluctant to shift places from the skilled stream to the family stream to reduce the partner backlog.

When I invited Julian Hill to comment for this article, he said he was proud that Labor, after taking office, had cleared a backlog of partner visa applications stalled for up to ten years or more by the “blatant discrimination” of former ministerial direction 80. “More recently,” he added, “it is true that demand for partner visas expressed through applications has been growing faster than the population.”
In July, home affairs minister Tony Burke issued a new ministerial direction, instructing the department to prioritise family applications lodged onshore ahead of those lodged offshore.

The change would have provided an incentive for partners to come to Australia as tourists on a visitor visa and then lodge their partner application here, enabling them to remain in the country on a bridging visa. This would have added to the tally of 412,000 people already living in Australia on bridging visas, another problem the government is struggling to manage.

In his Press Club speech Burke announced the government’s solution. In future, all visitor visas will be issued with a “no further stay” requirement. Burke put a positive spin on this, arguing that it will mean fewer visitor visa applications will be rejected because Home Affairs suspects the motivations of the applicant. So, he said, “while someone is waiting for a spouse visa to come through, their partner will be able to visit Australia on a regular basis.”
I doubt this will console couples separated by oceans. With onshore applications given priority, their future will be put on hold for even longer.

In July, the government also raised the hurdle for people seeking partner visas by increasing the cost by 25 per cent to $11,710. This is more than nine times what Canada charges for a spouse visa. High prices may delay some applications but will not deter committed couples from applying once they can afford to do so. In the meantime, they will have good reason to be upset and angry.
None of these changes will do anything to shorten the queue.

Given its political and legal constraints, the only obvious way for the government to issue more partner visas and shorten the queue is to take visas from other parts of the family program. This brings us to parent visas.

Unlike partner visas, parent visas can be capped and queued. The number of visas on offer this year is 7050, down from 8500 and a fraction of the average of 21,000 applications submitted annually over recent years.

Not surprisingly, the queue for parent visas is even longer than the queue for partner visas, though not growing as quickly. On 30 June 2026 more than 161,000 parent applications were stuck in the queue. Home Affairs advises new applicants that the processing time for a “contributory” parent visa with a price tag of $49,900 is fifteen years. The wait time for a standard parent visa — price tag $8665 — is thirty-three years.

Elsewhere, I’ve called this the parent conundrum. On the one hand, overseas-born Australians have a legitimate, heartfelt desire for parents and grandparents to join them here. On the other hand, governments have concluded that parents are not the kind of migrants Australia wants: they are old and likely to consume far more in services than they contribute to taxes.

Yet successive Coalition and Labor governments have refused to take decisive action. They won’t say an outright “no” to families hoping to bring parents to Australia, and nor will they increase parent places to match demand. The result is elderly applicants dying in their thousands as they wait in the lengthening queue. As the expert panel reviewing Australia’s migration program concluded in 2023: “Providing an opportunity for people to apply for a visa that will probably never come seems both cruel and unnecessary.”

Here is an option home affairs minister Tony Burke chose not to take. He could have ended parent migration altogether and shifted all 7050 parent visas to partners instead. This might have reduced the backlog of partner visa applications and would certainly have slowed its growth. It would be a more honest approach, since successive governments have made clear parents don’t match their image of the ideal migrant: young, healthy, skilled and fluent in English.

Why didn’t Tony Burke take this course? There would have been a political backlash of course, particularly from first-generation migrants in outer-suburban seats like his own electorate of Watson in Sydney’s southwest, and Labor’s political opponents would no doubt have cynically exploited it. But the more significant factor may have been cost. This might seem perverse. Governments don’t like parent migration because they see older migrants as a fiscal drag. But if it ended parent migration altogether, the government would be obliged — morally, if not legally — to refund the application charges already paid by 161,000 applicants stuck in the queue. This would amount to hundreds of millions of dollars.

A less dramatic option would be to freeze the parent program and announce that no new applications can be lodged until the current backlog has been processed. But this isn’t on the table either, and again perverse budgetary considerations play a role: Home Affairs would no longer receive the non-refundable first instalment charge of more than $6000 per applicant and would have to explain to Treasury how it was going to replace that forgone revenue. (It adds up to around $100 million annually if my back-of-the-envelope calculations are correct.)
When it comes to migration reform, partners and parents are not in view. They look likely to remain stuck in the too-hard basket, and the queues will grow even longer. •

Note: Once upon a time, I would have obtained the data used in this story by calling the immigration minister’s office or the immigration department’s media team. In recent years, though, I’ve been told the information I am seeking is not available, even though the department regularly updates the minister’s office on visa processing statistics and the data is routinely gathered for reports on the administration of the migration program (usually published long after I want to use it in an article). Now, Home Affairs offers a data request service and tries to finalise requests within thirty business days — this request took twenty-nine days — and also charges a fee. This year’s was $300, whereas last year’s request for much the same information cost only $90. When I queried the increase, I was told “the way the department charges has changed.”
